newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian drug lord denies leaning on lawmakers.
newsitem.headline: Colombian drug lord denies leaning on lawmakers.

text.p: Billionaire Colombian drug baron Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela has denied allegations that he attempted to coax congressmen to vote against legislation that could cost him a fortune.

Rodriguez, the Cali cartel kingpin known as "El Senor" ("The Man"), rejected the charges in a letter sent late on Monday from the maximum security wing of Bogota's La Picota prison to the Noticiero Nacional television news programme.

The programme on Monday aired what it said was a taped phone conversation between Rodriguez and his lawyer in which security officials said he pressed -- in coded or obligue language -- for the lawyer to win over lawmakers set to vote on a law that would allow the government to seize assets linked to Colombia's lucrative drug trade.

But Rodriguez denied referring to the so-called asset forfeiture law in the taped conversation and threatened to sue the news programme unless it retracted the report. "There's nothing more false and tendentious than this news report," he said, adding that the bugging of private phone conversations with his lawyer violated his individual rights and was aimed at "trying to sink me further into disgrace."

A police raid on the maximum security wing of La Picota on Sunday -- prompted by a guard's reported loss of his service revolver -- turned up videocasettes of sessions of Congress in which the proposed asset forfeiture law and legislation that would increase prison terms for drug lords were discussed.
In addition to marijuana and champagne and a dozen bottles of whiskey, police also discovered an official copy of the asset forfeiture law, printed on congressional stationery.

Ingrid Betancourt, a ruling Liberal Party lawmaker, charged in a speech in Congress on Monday night that some legislators had been offered $20,000 to $25,000 by Cali cartel emissaries to vote against the asset forfeiture law. She gave no names, but the law has been bogged down for weeks and a majority of lawmakers have said they will vote against the government's proposal that it take effect retroactively.

Its passage without retroactivity, which Justice Minister Carlos Medellin has said would be tantamount to legalising ill-gotten gains, could save traffickers hundreds of millions of dollars in real estate holdings and other assets.
